newsitem.title: UK: Major keeps Britons guessing about election.
newsitem.headline: Major keeps Britons guessing about election.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major kept Britons on tenterhooks on Friday about the timing of a general election but attacked the opposition Labour Party's devolution plans for Scotland and Wales and its willingness to cede powers to Brussels.

"Its policy of dispersing responsibility in all directions would make parliament a remnant of our democracy, a mausoleum to the nation state," Major told a conference of the Welsh wing of his ruling Conservatives in the village of Holywell.

Major's speech followed overnight interviews in which he gave apparently contradictory signals about whether he planned to call a snap election within weeks or wait until the end of his full term in May. The Conservatives lie 20 points behind Labour in opinion polls.

He did not address the question of an election date in his speech which concentrated on the Conservatives' support for the "Union" of the four countries that make up Britain. Labour plans mini-parliaments for Scotland and Wales.
"Once you set Wales against the north-east of England, Scotland against Wales...the strength of Britain will be sapped, our national purpose undermined," Major said.
"A thousand days of Labour government could ditch a thousand years of British history. It's a poor bargain -- better to keep the history and ditch Labour."

Major criticised Labour for its apparent sympathy for the idea of a "Europe of the regions". If European Union headquarters in Brussels began dealing with regions rather than nation states, its powers over Britons' lives was bound to increase, he said.
Major's speech, in which he said the Conservatives could make Britain "the best place in the world to live", came amid fevered speculation he could call a snap election for March 20 or April 10.
Late on Thursday, he told a television interviewer people should "sit back and not get too excited" about an election. Aides said it was a clear signal he had rejected a snap poll.
But asked in an interview with the Liverpool Daily Post what he would be doing on April 10, the fifth anniversary of his 1992 general election victory, he struck a different note.
"It depends whether we have had the election. I might be celebrating having won an election. I might be working to win an election," he said.
In the face of these confusing hints, political observers said the most likely date was still May 1 but that was by no means a certainty.

The only problem with this date for the Conservatives is that it would allow a parliamentary by-election to go ahead on February 27 in Wirral South, just a few miles (kms) from where Major was speaking on Friday.
The party looks set to lose this contest, caused by the death of legislator Barry Porter, who won the seat at the 1992 general election by over 8,000 votes.
That would put the Conservatives in a minority in parliament, increasing the risk of Major being forced to call an election at a time not of his choosing.

A defeat is possible, though unlikely, on Monday when parliament debates a Labour motion seeking the resignation of Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg over his handling of the "mad cow" disease crisis. Defeat could trigger a vote of no confidence.
